La Hire On Ellipse

GeometryCurvesConstructions
Game: This is a picture to explore: two dots outside an oval each send two lines that only brush the oval.
How to play: Drag A, B or a corner of the faint box, or focus a point and use the arrow keys. Press Put B on CD to see where the other line ends up.
Look for the math

Move the points around and the two chords keep a surprising link: put one point on the first chord and the other point lands on the second. Nothing about the oval's size or tilt seems to break it.

Two lines that only just touch

From a point outside the ellipse there are exactly two tangents. They touch at C and D, and the chord through those touching points is called the polar of A. If the oval has centre (cx, cy) and half-widths a, b, that chord obeys (x−cx)(xA−cx)/a² + (y−cy)(yA−cy)/b² = 1. The applet finds it by stretching the oval into a circle, taking tangents there, and stretching back; the test checks all four touching points against both formulas.

The claim on the page

The cut-the-knot page says: if B lies on CD, then A lies on EF. That is true exactly, not just nearly. In the formula above, swapping the roles of A and the variable point leaves the left side unchanged, so the two distances to the chords vanish together. The logic test confirmed the claim and its converse on 400 ovals and point pairs. The applet itself is less exact: its little eyes light only when the distance from A to the drawn chord EF is under one pixel, so that is what the status line reports too.

How this differs from the circle applet

The sister page La Hire's Theorem uses a circle and builds each polar by inversion — a point-and-line construction with perpendiculars — checking a 1.5-pixel gap. Here the polar is the chord joining the two tangent contacts, computed by the ellipse's own tangent routine, and the gap is 1 pixel. Both express the same reciprocity. This page adds a Put B on CD button (the applet only lets you drag by hand), keeps dragged corners from collapsing the oval, and simply stops drawing when a point moves inside, where no tangents exist.

Every non-degenerate conic

The page adds that the theorem works for all non-degenerate conics. That claim holds too: a conic has a symmetric equation in three homogeneous coordinates, and its polar relation is a symmetric product. If one point satisfies the polar equation of the other, the reverse follows at once — for ovals, hyperbolas and parabolas alike. An affine map that tilts or stretches an oval keeps this relation, which is why the four corner handles cannot break it.

Try this: press Put B on CD, then drag a corner of the faint box. As the oval changes shape, both chords move with it and A stays on EF.
